subject: how to use an R debugger to explore ggplot2?

messages.author: 59127c592feb1dac
messages.subject: how to use an R debugger to explore ggplot2?
parts:
Dr. Wickham,

I've read your book on ggplot2 but to better understand how ggplot works, I've downloaded the source code for the latest version of R and ggplot2 and I'm using Eclipse with StatEt to browse the source text. I also want to observe ggplot's behavior through the debugger the way I do Java code in Eclipse. (Even the Lisp machines I used back in the 80's had rich development environments.) However, I'm having difficulty finding an easy way to use a debugger to single step through various functions. In particular, the debugger seems to skip over expressions wrapped in a data environment, i.e., with(data, expr, ...). So if I want to see, for example, what stat_boxplot generates in its calculate() function, I can't seem to step through that code.

I'm an old hand at software design and development, but relatively new to R. I've looked at the introductory manuals and the papers on the internals of R and the R language, at a few files on debugging, and the FAQ warning at the end of Proto describing how to correctly invoke the debugger on its object methods. But I must be missing something.

What development environment do you use for the R scripts, how do you debug, and what else should I be reading?

Best regards,

Wayne Johnson

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: how to use an R debugger to explore ggplot2?
parts:
Hi Wayne,

I have to admit that since I have access to the ggplot2 source code, I
don't bother much with interactive debugging - I just stick in a
browse statement near where I think the problem is occurring.
Unfortunately debugging ggplot2 code is not easy because there is so
much indirection - often the error will be a consequence of something
that happened much earlier, and because my functions aren't very good
at recognising errors early (this is an unfortunate consequence of the
fact that I'm paid to do research, not software development).

So I don't know how to do better, but I do wish it was easier.

Hadley

parts:
I should mention that I am trying to do better. I think my recent
packages (e.g. plyr and stringr) have cleaner designs made up of
smaller functions that are easier to understand and decently
documented. Part of this improvement I credit to teaching statistical
computing - I make my students write a lot of code and reading all the
code and figuring out how to grade it have really improved my
understanding of what makes good code (draft rubric at
http://had.co.nz/stat405/assessment/code-rubric.pdf and style guide at
http://had.co.nz/stat405/resources/r-style-guide.html). I am also
trying to incorporate more automated testing in my packages, and to
that end have developed the testthat package (brief introduction
attached) which attempts to make testing as fun as possible so that I
actually do it.

Hadley

messages.author: 59127c592feb1dac
messages.subject: Re: how to use an R debugger to explore ggplot2?
parts:
Hadley -

Helpful responses from both you and Gerry, but not the answers I was hoping for. I've found your code clean and well organized. No complaint there (and it's good to see you promoting software engineering discipline with your students). However, reading code can take you only so far. A good debugger, tightly integrated with the source code editor, lets one quickly set breakpoints on source files, navigate in and out of functions, and selectively disclose details about variables and objects in order to observe runtime state and figure out who is doing what and when. It would be especially helpful here where so much behavior is parameterized by default.

Eclipse + StatEt doesn't provide that kind of environment. It outlines the source files and provides hyperlinks to navigate to the place where, for example, a function is defined. But it only establishes a pipe between it's console for R and the R application so that commands and responses can be exchanged. You cannot go into the source files and click on the lines in each source file where you would like to suspend computation once execution begins to have a look around. I suspect Emacs + ESS takes the same approach and has the same limitations, but if it does more I'll give that a try.

Thanks, again, for your response and  for making available a good reference implementation for understanding and sorting out the details underlying the GoG concepts.

- Wayne
